title: WHAT KIND OF DIGITAL PRODUCT COULD I CREATE?
content:
"Digital product" describes how something is delivered, not what the customer is actually buying. Before choosing a format, it helps to ask what kind of value you want to give them.

Someone who needs an explanation or plan might want a guide. Someone who repeatedly performs a task might benefit from a template, spreadsheet, checklist, or resource. Someone learning a skill may need structured instruction. A creator or business may pay for an asset they can use. In some cases, the useful thing is a digital tool or piece of software.

The goal is not to pick the format that sounds most impressive. It is to match the format to the problem.

DRAFT QUESTIONS
What do people ask you for help with? What have you learned to do? What information, system, shortcut, tool, or resource could save someone time, confusion, or effort? What could you realistically create and maintain?

When you have a direction worth exploring → PDF 07.
If creating your own digital product no longer appeals → PDF 05.

START WITH THE JOB, THEN CHOOSE THE FORMAT
Suppose you know how to help someone prepare financially for maternity leave. That knowledge could become a guide, spreadsheet, checklist bundle, course, calculator, or combination. Choosing the format first can force the idea into a shape it does not need.

Ask what the customer needs to get the result. If they need an explanation and plan, a guide may be enough. If they repeatedly organize information, a template may help. If they need demonstrations or practice, structured education may fit. If the value comes from performing a task, a tool may fit.

A direction is worth exploring when there is a plausible connection between a person, a problem or desire, and something digital you could create that helps.

FORMAT MATCHING EXAMPLES
"I know the steps but people need a clear sequence." -> A guide or short course might fit.
"People repeatedly build the same thing from scratch." -> A template, worksheet, spreadsheet, or resource pack might fit.
"People need examples they can adapt." -> A swipe file, asset pack, or template collection might fit.
"People need a task performed automatically." -> A software/tool concept may fit.

These are prompts for exploration, not rules. One problem can support several formats.

BEFORE YOU CHOOSE AN IDEA
You do not need to start with a topic you are "passionate" about. Useful product ideas can come from work you already know, a problem you solved for yourself, a process you repeat, a resource you wish had existed, or something other people regularly ask you to explain.

The strongest clue is not necessarily excitement. It is often a problem you understand well enough to imagine helping someone solve.

START WITH THE RESULT, THEN CHOOSE THE FORMAT

A common beginner mistake is choosing a format before choosing what the product is supposed to accomplish. "I want to make an ebook" sounds specific, but it still leaves the important question unanswered: what would someone buy the ebook to learn, solve, decide, create, or do?

The same useful information might become a guide, workbook, spreadsheet, template pack, short course, reference library, calculator, or simple software tool. The best format depends on what the customer needs to do with it.

If the customer needs an explanation, a guide may be enough. If they need to repeat a process, a template or checklist may be more useful. If they need to calculate or organize information, a spreadsheet or tool may fit better. If they need demonstration and practice, a course may make more sense.

You are not trying to choose the most impressive format. You are trying to choose the smallest format that delivers the result well.

WHERE IDEAS OFTEN COME FROM

Look for knowledge you have already organized for yourself. Think about processes you repeat, decisions you have learned to make, mistakes you can now help someone avoid, resources you have built because existing ones were frustrating, or subjects people already ask you about.

You can also start from a customer problem you understand even if you have not built the solution yet. The next guide uses ChatGPT to help turn those clues into a specific digital product direction.

A CONCRETE EXAMPLE

Suppose you are good at planning inexpensive family road trips. "Make a digital product about travel" is still too broad.

You might notice that parents repeatedly struggle to estimate driving days, meal stops, fuel, lodging, and activities without blowing the budget. Now there is a job for the product.

A short ebook could explain your planning method. A spreadsheet could calculate and organize the budget. A template pack could provide packing lists, stop-planning sheets, and itinerary pages. A mini-course could demonstrate the process. A simple tool could automate parts of the calculation.

Those are not five unrelated ideas. They are five possible ways to deliver a similar result.

This is why choosing the customer problem first matters. Otherwise beginners often choose the format they have heard people sell online and then search for something to put inside it.

WHAT OWNERSHIP MEANS HERE

If you create the product, you control the offer itself. You can decide what it contains, how it changes, how it is packaged, and, subject to any third-party rights or platform rules involved, where it is sold.

That does not mean every component must be created from nothing. You might use licensed fonts, stock assets, software, contractors, or other legitimate inputs. Ownership of the product and personally producing every ingredient are different questions.

YOUR NEXT STEP DEPENDS ON WHETHER AN IDEA HAS STARTED TO FORM

If one option now stands out, you do not need to keep brainstorming just because this guide contains several possibilities. Move into the ChatGPT exploration and develop that direction.

If nothing stands out yet, use the categories above as prompts for problems you understand, results you know how to help create, useful resources you could organize, or tasks people repeatedly struggle with.

The goal is not to select a format first and force an idea into it. The format should serve something useful you can imagine a customer wanting.

THE DECISION

Choose the digital-product direction that gives a customer a useful result in a format you would realistically create and maintain. Once one direction stands out, stop comparing categories and explore that specific idea.

WHERE TO GO NEXT
Once you have even a rough creator-owned digital idea, continue to PDF 07 and let the interview make it specific.
